newsitem.title: USA: US utilities struggle with cost of clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: US utilities struggle with cost of clean air rules.

text.p: Everyone in the U.S. electricity industry is convinced the stricter clean air rules proposed Wednesday by the Environmental Protection Agency are going to cost the industry a lot of money.
But none can yet say how much, and analysts warn against hitting the panic button until more is learned about the plan.
"We certainly suspect the cost is going to be in the billions (of dollars)," John Kinsman, manager of atmospheric science at Edison Electric Instutute said Thursday.
Washington-based EEI represents nearly 250 investor-owned utilities, which together produce about 75 percent of the nation's electricity.

"We're reviewing what EPA has put together. Very early preliminary data suggest that the approach they are looking at could cost up to $800 million for our system," said Steve Brash, spokesman for Cincinnati, Ohio-based Cinergy Corp, a major Midwest power supplier.
"We will be in the process of seeing if any of the additional information that has come out will allow us to revise that and to narrow that number," he said.
The rules set out by the EPA and backed by the White House seek to further cut ozone levels and, for the first time, set federal standards for soot.
Soot, or tiny air-borne particulates that can enter the lungs, are blamed by the EPA for 15,000 premature deaths a year and thousands of asthma attacks, especially in children.
A major source of both ozone and soot is fossil fuels, and the EPA's latest proposal cites coal-fired power plants as among the biggest industrial offenders.
Coal fuels about 50 percent of all U.S. power generation, compared with 22 percent nuclear, 10 percent natural gas, 10 percent hydroelectric, and two percent residual fuel oil.
The two main pollutants addressed in the EPA proposal are sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx).
About 29 percent of all NOx emissions can be traced to power plants, especially the coal-fired facilities.
"Selective catalytic reduction is what you need to get the big, 80 percent reduction of NOx. It's very expensive," said Kinsman.

To bring sulphur dioxide emissions in line with the EPA standards would require fitting smoke stacks with "scrubbers", a proven technology already widely in place, or switching to low-sulphur coal or natural gas.
Many of these steps were taken after the National Ambient Air Quality Standards were put in place in 1977.
While great strides have been made toward cleaner air nationwide, about 75 urban areas still have not met the 20-year-old air quality goals, Kinsman said.

Regulations were further tightened in the revised Clean Air Act of 1990, which roiled the automotive, refining and electricity industries in its bid to drive down harmful ozone levels in the lower atmosphere.
Phillip Giudice, a utility analyst with Mercer Management Consulting in Boston, said compliance with the 1990 Clean Air Act ended up costing power producers far less than was first feared.
"They said it would drive up the cost of power by 10 to 20 percent. But they came up with some very creative solutions, and power prices have not gone up at all," he said.
"Warnings of huge capital costs to the industry could be a case of Chicken Little crying 'The sky is falling' at this point," he said.

Pat Hemlepp, a spokeman for American Electric Power Co Inc,, said the ultimate cost to the industry simply could not be gauged at this time because the EPA will let the states work out how best to comply with the new standards rather than dictate a federal implementation policy.
"We can't put a number on (the cost) because the next step is for the states to submit their implementation plans. It's really up to the states," he said.
Congress has 60 days to review the standards, which would be implemented for smog beginning in 2004 and for soot probably at some later date.
The plan is already under attack from congressional leaders representing states with heavy industry.
